subject: dbms
name: Databases & SQL
tagline: Modelled data, queried declaratively, kept consistent
summary: A relational database stores data in relations with declared constraints, and queries it declaratively: you say what you want, and the optimizer decides how to get it. Most database skill is modelling well and then reading what the plan is doing.

sections.heading: Declarative means the plan matters
body: SQL describes the result, not the procedure. Two identical-looking queries can differ by orders of magnitude depending on whether the optimizer used an index, which is why reading EXPLAIN output is a core skill rather than an advanced one.
A missing index on a join or filter column turns a scan into a full table scan. An unselective index can be worse than none. Cost estimates, not rules of thumb, decide.
bullets: Model first: entities, keys, constraints
Normalize to remove redundancy, denormalize for measured read cost
Filter and join columns are the index candidates
Read EXPLAIN before optimising anything
Transactions carry the consistency guarantees

sections.heading: SQL is set-based
body: Thinking in sets instead of loops is the main translation. Aggregation with GROUP BY and HAVING, window functions for running and ranked values, and set operators for combining results cover most needs. Row-by-row processing in application code usually duplicates what one query could do.
The common performance mistake is the N+1 pattern: one query for a list, then one per row for details. A join or a single IN query replaces the loop.

keyPoints: SQL is declarative; the plan decides the cost
Read EXPLAIN before optimising
Index the filter and join columns
Think in sets, not row loops
Constraints are cheaper than application-side validation

examples.title: The N+1 pattern
examples.body: Loading a page of orders and then querying the customer for each one costs one query plus N queries. A single join, or one query with IN, reduces it to one round trip.

examples.title: Ranked results without a self-join
examples.body: A window function such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) produces ranks in one pass, replacing a correlated subquery per row.

mistakes: Optimising before reading the plan
Selecting star instead of the needed columns on wide tables
Storing comma-separated values in a single column
Assuming a query is fast because the table is small today
practiceTip: For every query you write, ask what index the optimizer would choose and why. If you cannot say, run EXPLAIN.

subject: dbms
name: Normalization
tagline: Remove redundancy by moving dependencies into their own tables
summary: Normalization reorganises tables so that each fact is stored once, which prevents update, insert and delete anomalies. The normal forms are a sequence of requirements about what a table's primary key determines.

sections.heading: The forms as a sequence
body: First normal form requires atomic values and no repeating groups. Second requires every non-key column to depend on the whole key, not part of it. Third goes further: no non-key column may depend on another non-key column, which means no transitive dependencies.
BCNF tightens the third form's dependency rule. In practice, reaching BCNF on every table is rarely worth the join count, and many production schemas stop at third normal form deliberately.
bullets: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF: no transitive dependency between non-key columns
BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key
Denormalize only for a measured read cost

sections.heading: The anomalies you are removing
body: Update anomaly: one fact stored in many rows, so changing it means many changes and inconsistency is possible. Insert anomaly: unrelated data cannot be recorded because something else is missing. Delete anomaly: removing one fact destroys another that had no other home.
Naming the anomaly a normalization prevents is the standard way to answer why it matters, and it is a more convincing answer than citing the form number.

keyPoints: 1NF atomic, 2NF no partial dependency, 3NF no transitive dependency
Normalization removes update, insert and delete anomalies
A functional dependency is what the forms are actually about
BCNF is stricter than 3NF and often unnecessary in practice
Denormalization is a performance decision, not a modelling one

examples.title: Splitting a course table
examples.body: A row holding course, instructor and instructor office stores the office once per student enrolled, so changing the office means many updates. Moving instructor details to their own table with a foreign key removes that anomaly.

examples.title: Transitive dependency
examples.body: Order rows storing zip code and city mean the city is determined by the zip, which is determined by the order key. City depends transitively, so it belongs in a zip-code table.

mistakes: Normalizing to BCNF everywhere without measuring the join cost
Storing multiple values in one column to dodge 1NF
Ignoring the anomalies and only citing form numbers
Treating denormalization as inherently bad
practiceTip: For each table you design, name the anomalies its structure prevents. That sentence is usually the whole normalization answer.

subject: dbms
name: Transactions & Concurrency
tagline: ACID is a contract, and isolation levels are a dial
summary: A transaction is a unit of work that is atomic, consistent, isolated and durable. Isolation is not binary: levels from read committed to serializable trade correctness guarantees against concurrency and throughput.

sections.heading: ACID, one promise at a time
body: Atomicity means all or nothing, implemented with an undo log. Consistency means constraints hold before and after, which is the application's definition as much as the database's. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other's intermediate states. Durability means committed data survives a crash, typically via a write-ahead log flushed before the commit returns.
Knowing which mechanism implements which property is what turns the acronym into an answer.
bullets: Atomicity: undo log
Durability: write-ahead log, flushed on commit
Isolation: locking or MVCC snapshots
Consistency: declared constraints plus application rules

sections.heading: Isolation levels and the anomalies they allow
body: Read committed prevents dirty reads. Repeatable read also prevents non-repeatable reads. Serializable additionally prevents phantom reads, and is the only level that behaves like sequential execution. Snapshot isolation in MVCC databases gives repeatable reads cheaply but allows write skew.
Read uncommitted allows dirty reads and is almost never appropriate. Choosing a level is a deliberate decision about which anomalies your application can tolerate.
bullets: Dirty read: reading another transaction's uncommitted write
Non-repeatable read: a row changes between two reads
Phantom read: a range gains or loses rows between reads
Write skew: two transactions read overlapping data and both write

sections.heading: Locking and MVCC
body: Two-phase locking acquires locks and releases them only at the end, which gives serializability but risks deadlock and reduces concurrency. MVCC keeps multiple versions of a row so readers never block writers, at the cost of version cleanup and some anomalies.
Deadlocks are detected or avoided by lock ordering, exactly as in the OS case, and the usual resolution is to abort one transaction and retry.

keyPoints: Atomicity via undo, durability via write-ahead logging
Read committed is the common default
Serializable is the only level equal to sequential execution
Dirty, non-repeatable, phantom and write skew are distinct anomalies
Two-phase locking gives serializability; MVCC gives cheap reads

examples.title: Transfer between accounts
examples.body: Debit and credit must both happen or neither, so they share a transaction. With serializable isolation, two concurrent transfers cannot interleave into a lost update.

examples.title: Report versus checkout
examples.body: A nightly report tolerates stale reads and can use snapshot isolation. A balance check that gates a payment needs repeatable read or serializable to avoid deciding on a value that changes underneath it.

mistakes: Assuming read committed prevents phantoms
Using higher isolation without measuring the contention cost
Retrying a deadlocked transaction without changing the lock order
Treating durability as guaranteed without a flush on commit
practiceTip: For each isolation level, write the anomaly it still permits. The table of level-to-anomaly is the entire answer.

mistakes: Left join then COUNT(*) inflating results
Filtering on an aggregate in WHERE instead of HAVING
Using DISTINCT to hide a join duplication bug
Joining on columns without indexes
subject: dbms

bullets: Inner: only matching rows
Left: all left rows, nulls on the right
Semi-join: filter by existence, do not duplicate
Anti-join: filter by non-existence
body: An inner join keeps only rows matching on both sides. A left join keeps every left row and nulls the right side where nothing matches, which is why counting after a left join can double-count.
Choosing between them is a question about which side is authoritative. If every order must appear even without a customer, a left join is required.
sections.heading: Joins decide the row count

bullets: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
Window functions keep rows and add computed columns
PARTITION BY sets the window, ORDER BY sets the order within it
Running totals are SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)
body: GROUP BY collapses rows into groups, and HAVING filters after the collapse while WHERE filters before. Window functions compute across a partition while keeping every row, which is how running totals and ranks are expressed in one pass.
Reaching for a correlated subquery where a window function would do is the usual performance loss.
sections.heading: Aggregation and window functions

practiceTip: Write every query twice: once with subqueries and once with joins or window functions. Compare the plans.
name: SQL Queries
summary: SQL expresses what to retrieve over sets of rows. Joins combine relations, GROUP BY aggregates them, and window functions compute values across a partition without collapsing rows.

examples.body: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at) gives a running total per customer in one pass, without a self-join.
examples.title: Running total per customer

examples.body: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY score DESC) then filtering on row number one gives the best row per group, replacing a correlated subquery.
examples.title: Top row per group

keyPoints: Inner join matches, left join preserves the left side
WHERE filters before grouping, HAVING after
Window functions compute without collapsing rows
Correlated subqueries are usually replaceable by a join
Count distinct to avoid double counting after a join

mistakes: Indexing every column on a write-heavy table
Wrong column order in a composite index
Expecting a hash index to serve a range query
Ignoring the plan and adding indexes on suspicion
subject: dbms

bullets: B-tree: equality and range
Hash: equality only
Composite: leftmost prefix rule applies
Covering: answers the query without a table lookup
Unique: also enforces a constraint
body: A B-tree index stores keys in sorted order with pointers to rows, so equality and range lookups are both logarithmic. A hash index maps a key to a bucket, giving O(1) equality but no ordering, so it cannot serve range queries.
A covering index includes every column the query needs, so the engine can answer from the index alone without touching the table. That is often the largest single win available.
sections.heading: What an index actually is

body: Every insert, update and delete must maintain each index, so write-heavy tables pay per index. An unselective index on a column with few distinct values is often ignored by the optimizer because a scan is cheaper.
The decision is data-driven: look at the query workload and the plan, then add the index that removes a scan. Indexing every column is a common well-meant mistake that slows everything down.
sections.heading: Cost and when not to

practiceTip: Before adding an index, run EXPLAIN and identify the exact scan you are removing.
name: Indexing
summary: An index is a separate structure that lets the engine find rows without scanning the table. A B-tree index serves range and equality queries, a hash index serves equality only, and each index slows writes and consumes space.

examples.body: An index on (last_name, first_name) serves queries filtering on last_name alone, but not queries filtering on first_name alone, because the prefix rule requires the leftmost column.
examples.title: Composite index order

examples.body: A dashboard query selecting id, status and created_at can be answered entirely from an index on those columns, removing every table access from the plan.
examples.title: Covering index win

keyPoints: B-tree serves equality and range; hash serves equality only
A composite index is used leftmost-first
A covering index avoids the table lookup entirely
Each index costs write throughput and space
Unselective indexes are usually ignored
tagline: Trade write cost and space for read speed
